title: Stream direct CSR Hadamard intersection without duplicate index maps
finding: TypedRelationBlock.hadamard eagerly materialized both sparse operands into Python dictionaries, built a set intersection of all coordinate keys, and sorted that set before multiplying common entries. The canonical CSR rows are already strictly sorted, so those duplicate maps and the extra set/sort were unnecessary memory and work before the bounded reference contraction completed.
primary_claim: The reference Hadamard contraction now intersects the existing sorted CSR rows with a direct two-pointer scan. It reads scalar values only for matching coordinates, preserves the existing exact semiring and operation-limit semantics, and removes the private indexed-entry helper made dead by the change.
gardener_decision: Delete the transient left/right dictionaries, key-set intersection, sort, and now-unused _indexed_entries helper. Traverse the already-canonical CSR row slices directly; do not introduce a planner, cache, alternate sparse block type, iterator abstraction, or cost-model layer.
acceptance: direct Hadamard does not read scalar values for non-intersection coordinates
direct Hadamard still refuses before multiplying when max_operations is exceeded
Boolean intersection output remains exact at the inclusive operation boundary
Fourfold subject, semiring, and identical typed-axis compatibility checks remain unchanged
no OwnerApproval, promotion, gate transition, or benchmark superiority claim is created

observed_jobs: contracts (3.12, 0): success with bounded Tensor/Forest diagnostic
verification.claim: Hosted CI is claimed only for the exact code/test revision above. Repository-wide evidence is collection-only, not a full-suite execution claim. No memory-speedup or benchmark superiority claim is inferred from removal of transient structures.

rollback: Revert the G1-TENSOR-01BD commits; Forest/Fourfold authority, persisted relation-block identities, wire contracts, semiring semantics, and public product surfaces remain unchanged.
